apsis.aphelion.summary: Earth is at its farthest from the Sun this year: {mln} million km. The difference between perihelion and aphelion is about 5 million km – and it is not what causes the seasons; the tilt of Earth's axis is.
apsis.aphelion.title: Earth at aphelion
apsis.perihelion.summary: Earth is at its closest to the Sun this year: {mln} million km. The difference between perihelion and aphelion is about 5 million km – and it is not what causes the seasons; the tilt of Earth's axis is.
apsis.perihelion.title: Earth at perihelion
conj.moon.summary: The Moon passes just {sep} from {body} – the pair is visible {visibility}, in {zodiac}. {blurb}. A striking naked-eye sight and a rewarding subject for a short telephoto lens.
conj.moon.title: The Moon meets {body}
conj.planets.summary: Only {sep} separates the two planets – less than the width of a finger at arm's length. Visible {visibility}, in {zodiac}. Angular distance from the Sun: {elong}°.
conj.planets.title: Conjunction of {a} and {b}
eclipse.solar_warning: WARNING: never look at the Sun without certified solar filters – sunglasses or exposed film do NOT protect your eyes.
elongation.summary: {body} stands {value}° from the Sun – the best chance this season to catch the planet {when}. {blurb}. Look for it low above the {horizon} horizon during twilight.
elongation.title: Greatest {direction} elongation of {body} ({value}°)
elongation.when.evening: in the evening, just after sunset
elongation.when.morning: in the morning, just before sunrise
launch.note: Launch dates slip often – check the current status before tuning into a webcast.
link.jpl: Object record in the JPL database
meteor.moon.bad: Unfortunately the Moon will be {illum}% illuminated and will drown out the fainter meteors – it is worth observing after it sets.
meteor.moon.excellent: Conditions are excellent – the Moon will barely interfere.
meteor.moon.some: A Moon {illum}% illuminated will brighten the sky a little.
meteor.summary: {description} At maximum, up to {zhr} meteors per hour in theory (the ZHR – under a perfectly dark sky with the radiant overhead; in practice usually several times fewer). The radiant lies in {radiant}. {moon} No equipment needed – just a reclining chair, warm clothes and a spot away from city lights.
meteor.title: {name} meteor shower peak
moon.summary: The Moon reaches {phase} in {zodiac}. Distance from Earth: {dist} km.
moon.summary.new: The moonless nights around this date are the best time of the month to hunt for galaxies, nebulae and the Milky Way.
moon.summary.supermoon: This is a supermoon – the disc is a few percent larger and noticeably brighter than usual. It looks most striking just after moonrise, low above the horizon.
neo.context.close: This is one of the closer approaches of the week.
neo.context.far: This is not a close encounter – it makes the list as one of the largest objects passing us this week.
neo.hazard.no: The pass is entirely safe – approaches like this happen regularly and are tracked as a matter of routine.
neo.hazard.yes: NASA classifies it as “potentially hazardous” – but that is purely a technical category for objects larger than about 140 m whose orbits come close to Earth's. No known object threatens us in the foreseeable future.
neo.size.building: roughly the size of a large apartment block
neo.size.hill: roughly the size of a small hill
neo.size.major: an object of this scale is a heavyweight in the catalogue of near-Earth asteroids
neo.size.tiny: an object this size would burn up in the atmosphere as a bright fireball
neo.size.tunguska: comparable in size to the Tunguska object of 1908
neo.summary: An asteroid with an estimated diameter of {dmin}–{dmax} m will pass Earth at {mln} million km, or {ld} times the Earth–Moon distance, travelling at {speed} km/s. For scale: {size}. {context} {hazard}
opposition.summary: {body} lies opposite the Sun – it rises at sunset, culminates around midnight and shines at its brightest of the season. Distance from Earth: {au} au ({mln} million km; its light takes {minutes} minutes to reach us). The planet is in {zodiac}. {blurb}.
opposition.title: {body} at opposition
planet.jupiter.blurb: binoculars will show its four Galilean moons
planet.mars.blurb: a distinctly orange point of light
planet.mercury.blurb: the hardest planet to catch – it never strays far from the Sun
planet.saturn.blurb: even a small telescope will show the rings
planet.uranus.blurb: at the edge of naked-eye visibility, easy in binoculars
planet.venus.blurb: the brightest point in the sky after the Sun and the Moon
season.december.summary: The shortest day of the year in the northern hemisphere. From now on the days grow longer – astronomical winter begins.
season.december.title: December solstice
season.june.summary: The longest day of the year in the northern hemisphere – the Sun reaches its highest point in the sky. Astronomical summer begins.
season.june.title: June solstice
season.march.summary: The Sun crosses the vernal point. Day and night are of nearly equal length, and astronomical spring begins in the northern hemisphere.
season.march.title: March equinox
season.september.summary: The Sun crosses the autumnal point. Astronomical autumn begins, and with it the aurora season – geomagnetic storms are statistically more frequent around the equinoxes.
season.september.title: September equinox
site.description: A daily updated guide to astronomical and space events: eclipses, conjunctions, meteor showers, rocket launches, aurorae and close approaches of asteroids.
site.title: AstroAlert – what's happening in space
sw.G1.advice: Aurora is possible over Scandinavia, Scotland and Iceland; farther south there is little to see.
sw.G1.label: a minor geomagnetic storm
sw.G2.advice: Aurora is usually visible from southern Scandinavia and Scotland, and in good conditions as a glow on the northern horizon from northern Poland and similar latitudes.
sw.G2.label: a moderate geomagnetic storm
sw.G3.advice: A real chance of aurora from central Europe – look for clear skies and a dark spot with an open northern horizon. A camera on a tripod will record it even when the naked eye sees only a grey glow.
sw.G3.label: a strong geomagnetic storm
sw.G4.advice: Aurora may be visible across central Europe, and high above the horizon at that. Storms like this happen a few times per solar cycle – worth dropping everything and stepping outside.
sw.G4.label: a severe geomagnetic storm
sw.G5.advice: An event on the scale of October 1989 or May 2024 – aurora visible even from southern Europe, with possible disruption to power grids, GPS and radio communication.
sw.G5.label: an extreme geomagnetic storm
sw.summary: NOAA forecasts a Kp index of {kp} for this day – {label} ({code}). {advice} Space weather forecasts are dependable one to three days ahead and can change from hour to hour.
sw.title: {code} geomagnetic storm – chance of aurora
